items.title: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
items.abstract: The post Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back. appeared first on ProPublica .
paras: On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum.

It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear.

But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother. That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.

Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches, frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time, he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to an online database.

Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about 200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont feature.
“I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I think the state needs to take this seriously.”

Just over a decade ago, state leaders seemed to be doing just that. In 2015, then-Gov. Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways.

The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016, the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036.

But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality projects and programs, Vermont’s cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double its annual pace.

Halfway through the two-decade timetable, Vermont has achieved only 35% of the goal, according to the state’s most recent estimates. And the steps that Vermont has taken to get there, such as upgrading sewage treatment plants, represent “low-hanging fruit,” Eric Perkins, a former EPA official involved in setting the target, wrote in an email in response to questions from Seven Days and ProPublica.

The culprit behind these blooms is phosphorus, an element that is an essential building block of life, present in all organic matter. But too much of it has been pouring into the lake from farm fields saturated with fertilizer and manure, dirty stormwater, and raw sewage from treatment plants overwhelmed by heavy rains. That has tipped the lake’s ecosystem out of balance, spurring the growth of microorganisms that turn shallow bays and shorelines into no-go zones.

Ingesting cyanobacteria-laden water can cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and liver damage, while skin contact can lead to rashes. Researchers have also detected possible links between chronic exposure to cyanobacteria and heightened risk of Parkinson’s disease and ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. The algae blooms can also deprive fish and other aquatic life of oxygen.

While some areas of Lake Champlain have seen incremental improvements in phosphorus concentrations and cyanobacteria blooms, other parts of the lake are getting worse. Seven of the lake’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015, a Seven Days and ProPublica analysis of lake monitoring data through 2025 shows. Four stations recorded higher average phosphorus levels over the past decade than in the decade before, including in the southern part of the lake and its northeast arm.

In September, the Department of Environmental Conservation reported to the EPA that in two northeastern sections of the lake most chronically plagued by phosphorus runoff, the state is not nearly on track to meet its targets. The department specifically acknowledged that it was not making enough progress in addressing stormwater runoff and that reductions in farm pollution in the Missisquoi River watershed have slowed since 2023.

Vermont shares the 120-mile-long lake with New York and Quebec, but it’s the source of about two-thirds of the phosphorus that flows into the water body. Agriculture is the largest polluting sector, while stormwater runoff from development, like urban parking lots and rural roads, contributes the highest amount of phosphorus per acre.

State agencies have repeatedly delayed taking more difficult and politically fraught action to crack down on pollution from farms, businesses and housing developments. Policies around them have encountered resistance from the dairy industry, property owners and lawmakers sympathetic to their interests.

The challenges in cleaning up Lake Champlain raise a salient question: If a small, conservation-minded state like Vermont can’t tackle this problem, what does that mean for other areas of the United States grappling with algae blooms in the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf of Mexico?
State officials counsel patience as they remind Vermonters it will take more time to solve the problem.

“We are moving apace with the commitments we’ve made, in terms of the projects, but it isn’t manifesting itself nearly as quickly in the lake monitoring data,” said Julie Moore, Agency of Natural Resources secretary. “This is a complex ecosystem, and we need to come at this work with a whole lot of humility.”

Leaders of the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets said it will take time for investments, such as programs to reduce soil erosion and help farmers upgrade their manure storage equipment, to pay off.

“The first five years, we were really developing an enormous amount of programs,” said Laura DiPietro, the agency’s water quality program director, but implementing them “doesn’t happen overnight.” She said she expects to see greater phosphorus reductions resulting from them in the coming decade.
But for van den Noort, the blooms are increasingly hard to ignore.
“The worst days ever are really, really bad,” he said. “Just as far as you can see, the whole bay is green.”
Unlike chemicals and heavy metals, which can be removed from lakes and rivers with dredging, phosphorus isn’t technically or economically feasible to extract.

So environmental regulators focus instead on limiting the amount of phosphorus that flows into the water each day. It’s like putting the lake on a diet. The EPA sets what’s known as the total maximum daily load, a target based on the agency’s determination of how much phosphorus the lake can absorb and remain healthy. To meet that goal, the state must cut pollution from agriculture, stormwater drains, roads, forests and wastewater treatment plants.

The EPA had set previous targets for Lake Champlain in 2002, but, concerned that Vermont wasn’t taking strong enough measures, the agency set tougher ones in 2016. For the first few years after those targets were updated, Perkins, who was then the EPA’s Vermont water quality coordinator, felt that the state was generally on the right track.

During his tenure, state agencies and lawmakers set up the Clean Water Fund to finance water quality projects and dedicated tax revenue streams to support it. They put in place stronger rules for fertilizer use and manure storage on farms. They created permit programs to limit stormwater runoff from roads and municipalities. That progress was reflected in a 2020 report card the EPA issued, acknowledging that Vermont had checked off all the milestones up to that point.
“Overall, I was very impressed with the level of commitment demonstrated by the state,” Perkins wrote to Seven Days and ProPublica.
By the time Perkins retired in 2021, he and colleagues at the EPA had become concerned about signs of lagging commitment by Vermont’s agencies to water quality enforcement on farms.

One clear opportunity to speed up phosphorus reductions, according to Perkins, is to ensure farms comply with required agricultural practices and avoid spreading manure before anticipated rainstorms, which has caused “major phosphorus runoff events.”

If the state and farm operators were to make that a priority, “it could likely make a big difference,” Perkins wrote. And the state could encourage that practice by overhauling its permitting system to tighten water quality requirements and enforcement for farms that keep animals confined in barns for long periods of time. Those farms are called concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs. In recent years, many small family dairies in Vermont have closed or consolidated into larger operations that would be considered CAFOs under federal law.

Yet Vermont has delayed action on an EPA directive to strengthen its approach to regulating CAFOs. Just across the lake, New York has used such permits for decades to ensure better environmental practices on larger farms. In Vermont, a recent state task force report recommended working to develop this program for another five years.
A second, related reform the EPA has recommended is to change who leads regulation of those farms.

Vermont has two different agencies that oversee farm pollution. The Agency of Agriculture regulates how farms handle waste on site, while the Agency of Natural Resources is responsible if runoff from that waste leaves the farm. This split responsibility has caused oversight problems, including lapses in following up on reported water quality violations with inspections and enforcement actions. Environmental advocates have long maintained that the agriculture agency has a conflict because it also has a mandate to promote the state’s farm sector.

This arrangement frustrates farmers, too. In a letter to Gov. Phil Scott earlier this year, owners of one Vermont dairy farm wrote that “the lack of alignment and clear communication between these agencies” places farmers in an uncertain position. “Many in the farming community feel caught in the middle of interagency disagreements, unsure which standards will ultimately govern their operations or how enforcement will proceed,” they wrote.

In interviews, officials at the two agencies acknowledged those communication problems but said that they have taken steps to improve how they share information on potential violations and coordinate more closely on inspections.

In 2024, the EPA ordered Vermont to consolidate the regulation of agricultural pollution under the Agency of Natural Resources, Vermont’s main environmental agency, which the EPA says has sole authority to administer federal Clean Water Act rules.

In a letter that year to Moore, the agency’s secretary, EPA Region 1 administrator David Cash noted that the EPA had monitored the situation in Vermont for well over a decade. “And despite having had ample time and opportunity to cure longstanding program deficiencies,” he wrote, “ANR has failed to do so.” Cash noted that the state has failed to give ANR “sufficient resources or operational authority” to regulate runoff from farms.
Hovering over this back-and-forth is the threat that the federal government could take over enforcement of water pollution rules from Vermont.

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.

Following the letter to Moore, the divisions between the two agencies were on display as they discussed their regulatory approach in internal emails obtained under Vermont’s Public Records Act by Seven Days and ProPublica. In a 2025 email, Agency of Natural Resources general counsel Catherine Gjessing reminded her counterpart at the agriculture agency and legislative counsel staff that “there are a significant number of farms that are in fact discharging without a permit” in violation of the federal Clean Water Act. She added that the two agencies had been working under this split responsibility arrangement, with the agriculture agency taking the lead, “for decades now and we are still not in compliance.”

In an interview, the agriculture agency’s general counsel, Steve Collier, said there was never “a Wild West situation where farms were not being regulated” and that his agency’s rules protected the environment. “Whether or not the Clean Water Act was being administered exactly as it should be is a different issue,” he said.

Outside of agriculture, Vermont has yet to fully implement a third EPA demand as well as the directives of its own Clean Water Act. That 2015 law mandated the Department of Environmental Conservation to require properties with 3 or more acres of paved surface, such as parking lots, to install systems to slow and capture stormwater runoff.

Five years later, when the department still hadn’t finalized this “3-acre rule” permit system, the EPA warned Vermont that it would have to give the state “a failing grade” if it didn’t do so by Sept. 4, 2020. Vermont met the EPA’s deadline but in 2025 passed a law pushing the date for getting permits to 2028 for properties in the Champlain basin.
And those property owners don’t need to make the stormwater upgrades until 2033.

For a quarter century, Steve Cushing has been advocating to clean up St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of Lake Champlain near the epicenter of Vermont’s dairy industry. Throughout that time, he listened as federal and state environmental officials came through town and pledged to act. “Expect a lot of progress 10 years from now in many segments of the lake,” one EPA official told him and his neighbors in 2015 .

A decade later, this summer’s cyanobacteria blooms in the shallow bay were some of the worst he’s seen in several years, he said. Since June, the public beach in the St. Albans Bay Park has mostly been closed to swimming.
“Overall, you can’t really see a big improvement in water quality in the bay,” Cushing said.

Public data supports that notion. Every three years the federally funded Lake Champlain Basin Program, which coordinates research and grantmaking across the lake’s watershed, issues a report summarizing its water quality monitoring.

Its most recent edition, from 2024, revealed “deteriorating” trends in the northeast arm of the lake for both phosphorus and cyanobacteria and no progress in Missisquoi Bay, a shallow stretch spanning the U.S.-Canada border that frequently suffers intense blooms.
That’s troubling, scientists and advocates say, because the failure to address new pollution is exacerbated by both historical pollution and the effects of climate change.

What scientists call “legacy phosphorus” has accumulated in soils and lake sediments after many decades of fertilizer use, manure spreading, deforestation and unregulated septic and wastewater systems.
“We are working on a system that’s been impacted by human activities for the past 150-plus years,” said Matthew Vaughan, the chief scientist of the basin program.

Climate change poses another headwind for the lake cleanup. Since 2003, cyanobacteria blooms have appeared earlier in the spring and later in the fall as temperatures rise, and even at lower phosphorus levels. The drought that hit Vermont in 2025 led to a spike in blooms, thanks to the combination of heat and low water levels. Meanwhile, downpours are turning Vermont’s streams and rivers into fire hoses of phosphorus-laden sediment: In just one week in July 2023, record-shattering floods pumped six months worth of phosphorus into the lake.
“All of this just makes it more urgent to do our part to address these water quality challenges,” Vaughan said.
Some state officials and researchers contend that phosphorus deposited in the lake bed and soil decades ago might play as significant a role in fueling algae blooms as today’s runoff.

But while legacy phosphorus remains a challenge, “I think it’d be wrong to just rely on that as the excuse,” said Eric Smeltzer, who worked for the Department of Environmental Conservation for 35 years, including as the state limnologist who monitors the health of Vermont’s lakes and ponds.

“The most important technical question about the Lake Champlain phosphorus cleanup is: Are these practices working? And if not, why not?” Smeltzer said. “How can it be done better? I think you can’t just explain it away based on time lags and legacy phosphorus forever.”

In reviewing the state’s data recently, one detail in particular jumped out to him, he said. Wastewater treatment still garners an outsize share of Vermont’s clean water spending, even though it has been clear for years that it’s not a major contributor of phosphorus, while agriculture and stormwater are.

Cushing traces the algae blooms back to the dairy farms that dominate the watershed and to regulators’ failure to “put any teeth behind” restrictions on manure spreading and other water quality rules.

Cushing, a former dairy farmer, has pushed for policy changes as a volunteer with the St. Albans Area Watershed Association and has led an effort to mechanically remove vegetation that contributes to the phosphorus problem in his overburdened bay.
At 78, he is now searching for someone to take over the weed removal effort. “I’m getting a little burned out,” he admitted.
Seven miles to the west, on the island of North Hero, van den Noort questioned this summer whether all the data he gathers is making any difference.
“If we really wanted to solve the problem, I think we’d have to make some tough choices,” he said. “I don’t think anybody wants to do that. It’s a head-in-the-sand thing.”

Every week, van den Noort drives up the western edge of Isle La Motte on his monitoring circuit, looking out over a stretch of water that is supposed to be one of the cleanest parts of Lake Champlain. On the worst days, a pea green broth of blooms stubbornly hugs its entire shoreline.

paras: Despite being an iconic part of Vermont’s landscape and a large source of the state’s drinking water, Lake Champlain has been polluted for decades. Phosphorus runoff from farm fields, rural roads, parking lots, stormwater drains and wastewater treatment plants flows into the lake, fueling algae blooms that frequently choke its bays and shorelines.

Vermont is halfway through a 20-year effort to clean up the lake. In 2016, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency established new, stricter requirements for reducing phosphorus runoff that the state must meet by 2036. But more than a decade in, after spending nearly a billion dollars, the state is lagging behind. Water quality has not improved dramatically, and in some parts of the lake, it is getting worse. This past summer algae blooms shut down swimming at public beaches in St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of the lake.

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to understand the reasons behind this lack of progress . We want to know how pollution in the lake is affecting Vermont’s economy and the lifestyles and livelihoods of Vermonters and visitors alike. How a French philosopher’s warnings about speed and power describe today’s AI race
items.abstract: Paul Virilio, a French philosopher, died in 2018. But his writings on technological ‘accidents’ help explain dilemmas the world faces today amid increasing use of artificial intelligence.
paras: With the race to build artificial intelligence systems smarter than any human has come a boom in “accidents.” In a safety test run by the company Anthropic , its own AI agent blackmailed an engineer to avoid being shut down. Criminals have used AI agents for data-extortion campaigns and to hack government agencies , banks and technology companies. In other tests, models have escaped from test environments into real organizational systems .

Several researchers who resigned from leading AI companies in 2026 have accused their employers of not taking the dangers seriously enough . In September, Bill Gates told “Meet the Press” that AI is “ powerful enough to drive events that can cause a billion deaths .”

Paul Virilio, a French philosopher, spent his career analyzing the relationships between technology, speed and power . He died in 2018 , well before generative AI and the fears about it reached their present pitch. But I doubt much would have surprised him.

As a researcher who studies AI-generated media and how people make sense of it, I find that three of Virilio’s ideas explain today’s AI moment better than anything written since. He argued that every new technology brings a new kind of accident into the world ; that speed takes away our time to think ; and that globally connected systems can fail everywhere at once.
Technology of speed

Virilio was born in Paris in 1932. When World War II began, his family moved to Nantes, a port city near the Atlantic. During the Nazi occupation of France, Germany began building the Atlantic Wall , a series of defensive fortifications stretching along the coast from Spain to Norway.

But in September 1943, when he was 11, Virilio saw what the wall could not keep out. American bombers aiming for Nantes’ port hit the city center instead , killing about 1,400 people and destroying more than 700 buildings in two raids.
“War was my university,” he told an interviewer . “Everything has proceeded from there.”

As a young man, Virilio spent years photographing the abandoned bunkers of the Atlantic Wall. The lesson he drew from them was about speed: The Germans had built a massive military fortification, yet the Allies had gone over and around it; the wall barely slowed them.
Walls were a technology of space, and the bombers were a technology of speed – inspiring his philosophical approach to understanding the world.
The ship and the shipwreck
As an adult, Virilio studied many more examples of technological failures, such as the Chernobyl power plant meltdown of 1986, the worst nuclear accident in history.

In his 2005 book “ The Original Accident ,” Virilio summed up his main idea in a simple sentence: “To invent the sailing ship or steamer is to invent the shipwreck.” The train invents derailment; the airplane, the crash; the nuclear plant, the meltdown. Every invention, not just dangerous ones, carries a specific kind of failure that did not exist before it.

In Virilio’s telling, the “accident” is not the result of bad luck added afterward. It is born at the moment of invention, even if the inventor cannot see it, because the invention will be used in ways they never imagined.

Virilio did not think such accidents could be avoided. But by carefully watching, he believed, people could contain failure and prevent catastrophe. He argued that societies tend to treat each disaster as a one-off, grieve it on television, and forget it, so that the next technology’s accident arrives as a surprise.

In 2002, he staged a Paris exhibition as a trial run for his plan to build a “Museum of Accidents.” Collecting information about shipwrecks, plane crashes, industrial disasters and financial crashes side by side, he argued, would show the pattern: that every invention has its failure and that failure can be anticipated .
AI has invented not one accident but several . Tech companies’ own incident reports form a sort of “museum” – but not an objective one.
Rule of the fastest
Virilio’s second key idea came from the Cold War. In 1977, he published “ Speed and Politics ,” written in a world where nuclear missiles could cross the planet in minutes.

He named the idea “dromology,” derived from the Greek word for a racecourse: “dromos .” Every age runs at the pace of its fastest machine, Virilio wrote, and whatever cannot keep up – including law, deliberation and conscience – drops out of the picture. There is “no democracy, only dromocracy”: the rule of the fastest.

AI can squeeze months of work into hours. In September 2026, Open AI announced that 10,000 of its AI agents had produced a proof of a math problem that had stood for a century – a problem two human mathematicians had spent a year trying to solve .

Virilio’s deepest fear about speed was not that people would fall behind machines, but that they would be absent from decision-making. Even when people attempt to stay in the loop, AI agents execute so quickly that human workers often fail to spot problems or malicious requests .
Everywhere at once
Virilio’s third idea is the “integral accident”: a failure that, because the same technology runs everywhere, happens everywhere at once .

During the 1990s, Virilio watched how satellite television, the internet and electronic markets let an event anywhere, such as a financial crash, be felt everywhere. He later predicted that in a networked world, integral accidents, not war, would be “ the continuation of politics by other means .”
AI has intensified how tightly connected the world is. It’s being used to help balance power grids , manage ships and harbors , and write hospital patient records .

Consider Anthropic’s Claude Mythos model, which finds security flaws in banking software faster than banks can fix them. Many financial institutions use the same software, so a criminal with such a model could break into multiple banks at the same time.
Hand on the lever

Virilio wrote that a society that lives only in the present makes accidents more likely . A society too busy to keep records of its past, or to think ahead, cannot learn from its failures and so repeats them.
I’d argue that that sentence points to three things worth keeping in mind.
The first is the record, kept by someone independent. Documents analyzing AI accidents should not be left only in the hands of the companies whose failures they document.
The second is the pause. Regulators, researchers and companies need the time and the authority to deliberate – and to halt a system, if needed, before it is released.

The third is skill. A skill is the present result of past practice. The more work people hand to AI because it is faster, the more they need to keep the ability to do that work themselves: to write the first draft, to check the sum by hand. These are the habits that let people verify what AI produces .

Virilio’s lesson is not to smash the machines, but to keep a hand on the lever – improving the chances that the accident, when it comes, can be seen, understood and reversed. Speed does not take the controls away, but it makes it harder for people to keep hold.

items.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
items.abstract: New research suggests that some ways that companies boast about their charitable giving are more effective at brand-building than others.
paras: People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount.

This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people . The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team.
Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts.

Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies.

To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal , a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank.

We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad.

Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke , a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000.

Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same.

Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes.
Why it matters

U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place.

Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026.

Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations . This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over.

Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off.
What still isn’t known
We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty.

It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense.
What’s next

Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder , a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.

items.title: A Feejee Mermaid on display in Colorado may shock and intrigue – but it’s no longer considered a ‘missing link’ on the evolutionary tree
items.abstract: All hoax – no science – the Feejee Mermaid startled American audiences that imagined it a real sea creature.
paras: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshipped Oannes , a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology ; and fairy tales such as “ The Little Mermaid ” have made this figure a pop culture icon.

During the 1800s, American showman P.T. Barnum brought the Feejee Mermaid to the American public. Presented at the American Museum, run by Barnum in Manhattan from 1841 to 1865 , as “ The Greatest Curiosity in the World ” and said to have originated in the “Feejee Islands,” the creature inspired debates about science and evolution. Some people believed it was a missing link in the evolutionary chain between aquatic and terrestrial life.

I recently viewed a Feejee Mermaid replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science as part of the “ Mythic Creatures: Dragons, Unicorns and Mermaids” temporary exhibit . As a folklorist , I’m intrigued by how this mermaid subverted Americans’ expectations that mermaids are alluring and how it sparked an interplay between science and myth.
Origins of the Feejee Mermaid

A Feejee Mermaid is a type of traditional art form that originated in Japan and the East Indies more than 400 years ago. It came to Americans in 1842, when Barnum claimed to display a “specimen” at the American Museum in New York City.

In the Japanese version, the lower half was a fish attached to an upper half of a monkey or made of papier-mâché. Barnum’s was a mixture of a monkey and a fish, but the replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science has a papier-mâché upper half. Feejee Mermaids were often preserved by being coated in clay .

Mammalian-fish hybrid creatures have a role in Japanese folklore through the ningyo , which are a mermaidlike yokai, a supernatural being thought to have the power to either curse or grant eternal life. Unlike Western mermaids, ningyo were grotesque.

The Feejee Mermaid that became part of Barnum’s exhibition was created by a Japanese fisherman in the early 19th century. He claimed to have caught the specimen and said it prophesied a sterility epidemic. The only cure for the townsfolk, the fisherman said, came through owning a picture of the mermaid.
Samuel Barrett Eades, an American sailor, purchased the Feejee Mermaid and willed it to his son, who then sold it to Moses Kimball , a curator at the Boston Museum, in 1842.
In his autobiography, Barnum details the scheme he devised after Kimball showed him the Feejee Mermaid.

Barnum sent letters to newspapers, describing how a “Dr. Griffin,” who was really his hoaxing accomplice Levi Lyman, was in possession of the mermaid skeleton. He further spread the word by distributing thousands of pamphlets throughout New York City that detailed when the mermaid would be on display and highlighted the seductive nature of mermaids.
However, when the public arrived at the American Museum, much to their surprise, they found Barnum’s grotesque version.

Barnum himself described it as “an ugly dried-up, black-looking diminutive specimen, about three feet long. Its mouth was open, its tail turned over and its arms thrown up, giving it the appearance of having died in great agony.”
Sideshow gaffs and American folklore

The Feejee Mermaid on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, and owned by the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, may or may not be the one shown by Barnum. The museum says it is a replica.

The original was likely destroyed or disfigured in a fire at Barnum’s museum or the Boston Museum. The object on display looks quite different compared to original descriptions of the Feejee Mermaid. As originally shown, it was said to be much more monkeylike, and artistic renderings of it from the period matched Barnum’s descriptions.

Feejee Mermaids, as displayed in America, are characteristic of a “ sideshow gaff ” that interested Victorian audiences due to debates about evolution and science. In fact, 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus had left space for mermaids in the evolutionary tree . The Feejee Mermaid, as it blended human and animal characteristics, folklore and science, spectacle and empiricism, displays how a monstrous hoax inspired fierce intellectual debates in 19th-century America.

items.title: NASA’s Swift Observatory has burned up in the atmosphere – the indispensable telescope helped astronomers track fast-moving events in space
items.abstract: The Swift Observatory allowed astronomers to study events that happen quickly in the universe, such as stars exploding.
paras: A 22-year-old space telescope lost its fight against gravity and came crashing down to Earth on the morning of Nov. 4, 2026, above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory had been the go-to telescope for observing astrophysical events that happen quickly, such as supernovas . Its onboard instruments allowed it to contribute greatly to many subfields of science.
Swift was not classified as a flagship observatory, like the Hubble Space Telescope or Chandra X-Ray Observatory , but it left behind a legacy that will not swiftly be forgotten.

The Swift Observatory first came onto the scene in 2004 when NASA launched it into low Earth orbit . Originally called the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, its purpose was to move quickly to follow up on explosive events called gamma-ray bursts and their afterglows using its three onboard telescopes.

Swift’s name is not an acronym. Instead, it refers to its speed and likens the observatory to the bird . It could rotate and move quickly to observe transient events , which are events that happen quickly and fade away.
Watching for gamma-ray bursts

Gamma-ray bursts are the most explosive and energetic events in the universe. Scientists theorize they come from the explosions of large stars or mergers of a very dense type of star called neutron stars . Gamma-ray bursts, as the name implies, release large bursts of gamma-rays, but as these explosions fade, they lose energy. Scientists can spot remnants of gamma-ray bursts by looking for X-rays and optical light as the gamma rays themselves fade.

Swift’s burst alert telescope could see light in the gamma-ray portion of the electromagnetic spectrum , so it searched directly for gamma-ray bursts. Its X-ray telescope and ultraviolet-optical telescope could measure the resulting afterglow of X-ray and UV light these events produced as they faded.

What set Swift apart was its ability to do what’s called slewing: In order to follow up on transient events, it swiveled its telescopes around quickly and could cover 50 degrees in less than 75 seconds . Comparatively, it takes Hubble about 15 minutes to turn 90 degrees .
By 2015, just 10 years after science operations started, Swift detected its 1,000th gamma-ray burst .
Beyond gamma-ray bursts

Swift’s ability to slew quickly allowed it to detect more than just gamma-ray bursts. Its onboard instruments could detect anything that changes quickly in the sky, including supernovae and X-ray flares from binary stars , which are two stars bound by gravity that tend to interact with each other. It could also detect the electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational waves , which result from large distortions in space-time, such as the merger of dense objects such as black holes and neutron stars.

In 2008, when observing another supernova, Swift by chance detected a slight rise in X-rays , which preceded a supernova explosion. This initial increase in X-rays represented the earliest phase of supernova evolution ever observed. Swift’s extensive alert network notified astronomers all over the world who were able to point other space- and ground-based telescopes at the supernova to follow up and obtain even more data.

Then in 2017, when the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – whose principal investigator Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics – detected high-energy neutrinos , Swift was able to help localize their source. Neutrinos are massless particles that do not interact with most matter. This property makes it hard for physicists to detect them and pinpoint their source. Scientists know that astrophysical events can emit them, and they used Swift to connect these neutrinos to a very energetic supermassive black hole at the center of its galaxy .

In 2025, Swift detected a compound called hydroxyl on the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS , indicating the presence of water. This result may help answer the question of how Earth obtained water on its surface. Some theories propose that comets and interstellar objects bombarded the Earth in the early solar system and deposited water.
A failed recovery mission

Swift’s journey took a turn in 2024 and 2025, as the Sun became more active . These years were in a period known as a solar maximum , when more solar flares, or explosions on the surface of the Sun, released matter and high-energy particles that hit Earth’s atmosphere .

Because of this increase in space weather, many people as far south as Pennsylvania were able to see the northern lights. While this activity produced jaw-dropping views, it also exerted pressure on satellites. Solar particles can exert a small force on whatever they hit, and when there are many, that force multiplies.

This force pushed against Swift, which lived in low Earth orbit at about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface. The telescope eventually reentered the atmosphere, where drag pulled it down toward Earth.
NASA partnered with a company called Katalyst Space Technologies and launched a mission to boost Swift back into its orbit on July 3, 2026.

Unfortunately, this mission failed, and Swift reentered and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere in early November. The observatory didn’t hit the surface fully intact. Instead, it mostly burned up on its way in.

The loss of such an observatory is a tough blow to the astronomical community, which was gearing up to use the satellite in conjunction with the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory . However, astronomers will continue to remember Swift’s team and their countless accomplishments and discoveries.

items.title: How space weather powers auroras in the sky and threatens power grids on the ground
items.abstract: When an aurora lights up the sky, electric currents can also flow through the ground beneath your feet.
paras: An aurora is one of nature’s most spectacular light shows: It looks like green or red curtains rippling across the night sky. When viewed from the ground, this colorful display might seem far away and disconnected from anything happening on Earth’s surface.

But while these beautiful displays are part of a much larger process known as “space weather” – changes in Earth’s space environment caused by activity from the Sun – they’re closely connected to electric currents that can flow through the ground under your feet.

Space weather can create a spectacle in the sky, while also driving electric currents that can damage power grids and other technological systems on the ground. Space physicists like us want to understand how space weather can affect infrastructure on Earth.

Our research shows that a single space weather event called a substorm , during which energy is released tens of thousands of miles away from Earth, can affect the ground within minutes. The strength of the impact can vary from place to place depending on the latitude and the structure of the soil and rock below your feet.
From solar storm to substorm
Earth is constantly immersed in the solar wind : a stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun. Occasionally, the Sun releases a much larger eruption called a coronal mass ejection .

This cloud of charged particles and magnetic fields does not simply “hit” Earth and immediately cause power-grid failures. Instead, it can set off a chain of processes in space that can pose a threat to power grids .

First, when the coronal mass ejection reaches Earth, the charged particles and magnetic fields it carries interact with Earth’s magnetosphere . The magnetosphere is the region of space around Earth dominated by its magnetic field.

If the coronal mass ejection’s magnetic field is oriented in a certain way, it can connect with Earth’s magnetic field on the side facing the Sun. The solar wind then carries these connected field lines around Earth away from the Sun and stretches them far out into space behind Earth. This process forms a long region of stretched magnetic field lines called the magnetotail.

Magnetic energy builds up in the magnetotail as the solar wind continues to push the field lines farther into space – until they come close enough to reconnect . Then, the stored energy is released in an explosive process known as a substorm . This release occurs on the side of Earth facing away from the Sun, roughly 28,000 to 40,000 miles (45,000 to 65,000 kilometers) from Earth.

During the substorm, energetic particles shoot along the magnetic field lines toward Earth. When these particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere, about 56 to 93 miles (90 to 150 kilometers) overhead, they produce the glowing aurora.
These energetic particles also drive strong electrical currents in Earth’s upper atmosphere . Rapid changes in these currents can cause Earth’s magnetic field at the ground level to change sharply.
These changing magnetic fields can induce electric currents in the ground and in power lines, potentially damaging transformers and tripping circuit breakers.
From the magnetotail to Earth’s surface
Our team wanted to find out how closely the aurora is linked to disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field and how long it takes for a disturbance released in the magnetotail to reach Earth’s surface.

We examined two auroral events in detail by combining data from NASA spacecraft – including THEMIS, time history of events and macroscale interactions during substorms , and NOAA’s GOES, geostationary operational environmental satellites – with data from a dense network of magnetometers across Arctic Canada that measure changes in Earth’s magnetic field at the ground. These changes in the magnetic field can drive electric currents in the ground and power lines.

The observations revealed a clear sequence. When these stretched magnetic field lines on the nightside suddenly reconnected, the spacecraft recorded an abrupt change in the magnetic field and a burst of charged particles moving toward Earth. About seven minutes later, the magnetic field at the ground began to change rapidly. The effects of this energy release, tens of thousands of miles away, reached Earth’s surface within minutes.
The aurora and ground disturbance do not appear everywhere at once. In our observations, they began at lower latitudes and then spread toward the North Pole over the next 20 to 30 minutes.

Nearby geomagnetic stations, however, often recorded very different responses. Stations tens to hundreds of miles apart could see strong magnetic swings at one site and weak ones at another. The difference depended on the strength of currents in Earth’s upper atmosphere and local conditions – including how electrically conductive the upper atmosphere is overhead and how conductive the ground beneath the magnetic station is. This atmospheric conductivity can vary with sunlight and auroral activity, while ground conductivity depends on local geology and moisture levels.
Seeing a spectacular aurora does not automatically mean the ground beneath it is experiencing the strongest magnetic disturbances or electric currents.
When the aurora becomes a grid problem

History shows that space weather poses a real risk to space and ground infrastructure. During a March 1989 geomagnetic storm, people witnessed spectacular auroras as far south as Texas, while rapid changes in magnetic fields contributed to the collapse of the Hydro-Québec power system . More than 6 million people lost electricity for about nine hours on a cold winter night. With the city lights extinguished, the aurora appeared even more spectacular.

A similar combination occurred during the Halloween storms of October 2003. Auroras illuminated skies across Europe, while geomagnetically induced currents contributed to a blackout affecting about 50,000 people in Malmö, Sweden.

Recently, during the May 2024 geomagnetic storm – the strongest in over two decades – geomagnetically induced currents stressed the power grid in southern Sweden, forcing a transmission link to disconnect and temporarily interrupting the flow of electricity through that part of the grid.

Space weather forecasts can warn power grid operators hours before solar activity reaches Earth, giving them time to monitor grid conditions and prepare for possible disruptions. But the effects of substorms, including potential risks to power grids, develop after the solar wind interacts with Earth’s magnetic environment. Our research shows that these effects unfold on timescales of minutes.

The next time the aurora ripples across the night sky, remember that the colorful light shining overhead is only one part of a larger process. Tens of thousands of miles away, an explosive release of magnetic energy may have just taken place. Within minutes, its effects can begin to reach the ground.
The beauty of the aurora and the risk of power-grid disruption from invisible currents above and below are two faces of the same space weather event.

items.title: Are schools a great equalizer? They help kids catch up, but wealthier children still pull ahead
items.abstract: By some measures, schools are a great equalizer for children coming from different backgrounds. But this isn’t the full story.
paras: In 1848, the education reformer Horace Mann called public schooling “the great equalizer of the conditions of men.” More than 175 years later, education scholars are still arguing about whether he was right.

Some research finds that a child’s family background shapes their academic achievement far more than schools do . Other work finds that schools narrow academic achievement gaps that would otherwise be even wider .

A classic study following Baltimore children in the 1980s found that low-income and wealthier kids learned at similar rates during the school year . Achievement gaps grew over the summer, when some children read with parents, visited libraries and went to camp, while others didn’t have those same opportunities. How much summer learning loss exists is still an open question.

But the larger point holds: Gaps between rich and poor children in reading and math skills are already large on the first day of kindergarten , driven by factors outside of K-12 schooling. For a given group of students, those gaps then stay about the same size through the school years.
I am a scholar of education policy who studies the different factors that shape students’ learning, including teachers and the quality of their instruction.

Instead of measuring how much students learn at school, as is often the case, my colleagues and I recently measured what students receive in and out of school : the school funding, education support services and time that schools, government programs and families put into each child.
By some measures, schools really are an equalizer for children from different backgrounds – but this finding has its limits.
A gap that starts early in childhood

In our 2026 study , we combined data from 10 nationally representative government surveys to track 77 kinds of investments, as we call them, that contribute to raising and educating children. This includes teachers, tutoring, housing, food and childcare. We also measured factors that don’t have a direct cost, such as the time parents and caregivers spend reading with children.
We put a dollar value on each factor – valuing parents’ time at the average U.S. hourly wage, for example – so we could add them up and compare what children from different backgrounds receive.
Counting government investment, family spending and the time parents spend with their children, the average child in the U.S. receives about US$502,000 from birth to age 18, our analysis shows.
The gaps in how much different children receive start early.
Before age 5, children from the poorest fourth of families receive about $44,000 less in total investments than children from the richest fourth – marking a gap of 24%.
Most of that early difference comes from housing and childcare costs.
However, a striking pattern emerges as children transition into elementary school. The gap in total investment between the richest and poorest children is cut in half, from 24% to 12%.
For Black children, the benefit of starting school is even greater. Investment gaps between Black and white children shrink from 20% in early childhood years to 7% once kindergarten begins.
This matters because research shows that more school spending improves students’ achievement and long-term outcomes , especially for those from low-income families .
So why don’t achievement gaps close during the school years?
Catching up vs. getting ahead
Part of the answer is what money buys.

Our research shows that once children are in school, those from the lowest-income families receive 72% more in tutoring and 68% more in special education than those from the highest-income families, and Black children receive more than twice as much tutoring as white children.
These services are meant to help students catch up. A dollar spent catching up is not the same as a dollar spent getting ahead.

Tutoring has long been one of schools’ main catch-up tools, and since the pandemic, schools have leaned on it more than ever . It’s a reasonable bet. Studies that randomly assign students to tutoring find some of the largest test-score gains of any school program .

Schools serving many low-income students have long been able to use federal Title I money for tutoring . Pandemic relief money made a bigger push possible. Congress sent schools nearly $190 billion , and the largest round was divided among districts the same way as Title I money , so high-poverty districts got more.

By 2022-23, more than a third of public schools offered “ high-dosage” tutoring , meaning frequent sessions in small groups. Schools serving more low-income students and students of color were more likely to offer it .
But for many low-income, Black and Latino students, tutoring wasn’t new.

In our data, collected from 2014 to 2021, about 17% of school-age children were being tutored, including 25% of Black children and 19% of Latino children, compared with 14% of white children. For Black, Latino and low-income children who received tutoring, over 75% got that support from public schools.

Early in the recovery, at least, the share of students getting tutoring didn’t appear to grow much. A nationally representative survey of parents in fall 2022 found about 15% of students were being tutored.

Meanwhile, the pandemic widened achievement gaps. Students in high-poverty districts still trail those in wealthier districts by more than students in the same grades did before the pandemic. Schools leaned harder on catch-up help that low-income, Black and Latino students were already getting. Federal relief money did help high-poverty districts recover . But even with that help, gaps remain wider than before the pandemic.
Who gets ahead
Catch-up help is only half the picture. Wealthier children also get more of the resources that help them pull ahead, in school and out.

Some studies show, for example, that low-income students and students of color are more likely than richer, white students to have newer, less experienced teachers . Our study documents the same pattern.
The differences are even starker outside of school.
In our data, wealthier families invest far more in music lessons, sports and other activities that can help kids get ahead.

Related research shows that by 2024, the richest 10% of families spent more than 13 times as much per child as the poorest quarter on childcare, education and extracurricular activities – up from about three times as much in the early 1980s.
Equal spending isn’t enough
Our findings show that public education is the main reason the investment gap between rich and poor children shrinks once kids turn 5.

But equal spending is not equal opportunity. Much of the extra school spending on low-income, Black and Latino children goes to making up for gaps that opened before they started school. Meanwhile, wealthier children keep getting more of the experienced teachers and enrichment that help them pull ahead.

If schools are going to be a true equalizer – closing gaps, not just keeping them from growing – more catch-up help won’t be enough on its own. These students also need more of what helps their wealthier peers get ahead. And because the widest gaps open before kindergarten – in housing and childcare, where public support is thinnest – closing them can’t be left to schools alone.

items.title: Tracing the recruitment trap behind Russia’s war
items.abstract: Bangladeshi men paid agents for Russian jobs and ended up on the front lines. Families wait for bodies and answers, and they want the recruiters behind it in a courtroom.
paras: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation , he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine . He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten , he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries . Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines .
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation ( ORF ). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted , while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy . Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds . Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit ( RMMRU ), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training ( BMET ) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited ( BOESL ) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe ; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.

paras: Egypt convicted Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations, and ordered it closed
Originally published on Global Voices
Lina Attalah. Photo from Mada Masr website, used with permission.
A crackdown on independent media in Egypt is escalating.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh , a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.

The six-person team was forcibly disappeared , illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news. They remain in pretrial detention.

The crackdown then reached Mada Masr , one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah. On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.

The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license, in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial. She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later. The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.

According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected. The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.

Mada Masr was founded in 2013 as an independent, critical, investigative outlet. In another decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region. It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.

Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism. At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday, October 30, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.” A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.

“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about. But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads. It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.” It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.

In an op-ed published on October 26, the Mada Masr team wrote that “in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday.”

They added: “There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism.”

And: “We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small us, Mada Masr, but a much bigger we.”

In Egypt, journalists who documented torture, political imprisonment, and security crackdowns now face courts that process them quickly and unfairly, under a licensing scheme that has left applicants without an answer for years.
For journalism to be free, that licensing scheme and its chilling effects on access to information, knowledge production, and critical voices in Egypt and beyond must be stopped.
